task.goal: Teach beginning musicians to hear and correct uneven rhythm in a group rehearsal.
hard_constraints: One instructor, eight beginners, three 30-minute sessions, and no recording app.
Do not single out a learner publicly or require extra home equipment.
Separate tempo drift from missed beats and check improvement on an unfamiliar pattern.
task.available_resources: Clapping, metronome already owned by instructor, paper marks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Predict the pulse through silent gaps
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: learners maintain an internal pulse while the metronome briefly disappears, then use its return to hear tempo drift. Counting positions separately helps distinguish drift from missed beats. This could work by making two different errors audible: the whole pulse moving versus an expected clap being absent.

Use one instructor, eight learners clapping together, the existing metronome, and paper showing eight numbered beat positions. Explain that everyone is testing a group skill; give only group feedback and never request individual demonstrations. Assume learners can hear the metronome and understand a steady spoken count. Start slowly enough for comfortable participation.

Session 1, 30 minutes: spend five minutes establishing pulse; five hearing instructor demonstrations of acceleration versus an omitted clap; fifteen alternating eight-beat group clapping with metronome-supported counting; and five discussing what changed. An omitted clap leaves its numbered position intact: continue counting rather than restarting.

Session 2: spend five minutes reviewing, fifteen alternating audible clicks with short silent intervals while learners continue clapping, five diagnosing examples, and five reflecting. The instructor mutes and restores the running metronome if possible. Otherwise, learners stop clapping for selected beats while clicks continue; this simpler version provides less evidence about independent pulse maintenance. Diagnose drift from repeated claps progressively separating from clicks; diagnose omissions from empty expected positions followed by correctly placed claps.

Session 3: spend ten minutes on longer gaps, ten alternating full clapping and paper-marked rests, and ten on the unfamiliar-pattern check below. Correction cues are specific: ‘keep the spacing’ for drift and ‘keep counting through the empty position’ for omissions. Group sound can conceal individual difficulties, so this supports group improvement without establishing individual mastery.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At the start and end of session 3, compare two previously unused eight-beat patterns with equal numbers of claps and rests. Randomly choose their order. For each, hear one supported attempt and one short silent-gap attempt. On paper, tally group omissions separately from progressive displacement against returning clicks; mark unclear cases as uncertain. Compare with ordinary continuous-click practice of equal duration. If silent-gap practice produces no clearer return alignment, or increases omissions, its proposed benefit is unsupported at this difficulty. One group and two patterns provide only a small practical check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Build rhythm around a shared pulse role
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: separate keeping time from producing the rhythm, then rotate those responsibilities. A steady subgroup provides an audible reference against which the other subgroup can hear whether its rhythm accelerates, slows, or loses an event. Reducing simultaneous demands may help beginners correct one problem at a time.

Use the instructor’s metronome, clapping, and paper strips with eight numbered positions. Four learners clap every beat softly; four clap only marked positions. Switch roles frequently, assign roles by seating rather than ability, and describe both as equally necessary. Nobody performs alone. This assumes the two sound layers remain distinguishable; the pulse group can clap softly while the pattern group claps at ordinary volume. If the room is too loud, shorten turns and lower both groups’ volume.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes establish a shared pulse, five hear instructor examples of drift and omission, fifteen practise the two roles with frequent switches, and five review. Keep the metronome audible. Teach that an omitted clap does not remove a beat: rejoin at the next numbered position. Drift means successive claps move increasingly ahead of or behind the reference.

Session 2: five minutes review, twenty alternate short supported and unsupported rounds, and five reflect. Before each unsupported round, establish the pulse with the metronome; restore clicks afterward to check whether the pulse subgroup itself drifted. If it did, reset together rather than treating its timing as authoritative. For omissions, simplify the marked pattern while retaining eight positions; for drift, return briefly to all-beat clapping.

Session 3: ten minutes rotate roles on familiar patterns, ten bring everyone together on the same pattern, and ten test unfamiliar patterns. The intended outcome is transferring the reference-pulse habit into full-group playing. Its main limit is dependence on the pulse subgroup: success during divided roles may disappear when everyone must manage both timing and pattern.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use two unfamiliar patterns matched for length, clap count, and rests. Practise one for three minutes with divided roles and the other for three minutes with everyone clapping together, using equal metronome support. Then perform each with everyone together, checking against clicks. The instructor tallies omitted events and progressive timing displacement separately, without naming learners. Choose pattern assignment by a simple draw. If the divided-role pattern performs no better once the pulse subgroup is removed, the transfer mechanism is unsupported. Pattern differences and collective masking limit conclusions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Hear the error, choose the repair
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: teach an explicit listening decision before asking for correction. Beginners practise distinguishing ‘the spaces changed’ from ‘an event disappeared,’ then select the matching repair. This may prevent a missed clap from causing a restart or rush, and prevent tempo drift from being treated merely as a counting mistake.

The instructor uses clapping demonstrations, the existing metronome, and paper marked ‘spacing,’ ‘missing,’ and ‘unclear.’ Learners point privately to a mark held close to themselves; the instructor reports only group trends. All performance remains collective. Assume the instructor can demonstrate the two errors clearly enough at a slow tempo. Mixed or ambiguous errors are labelled unclear rather than forced into a category.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes establish eight steady beats; ten compare instructor demonstrations against audible clicks; ten alternate listening decisions with group imitation of a correct version; five review. Demonstrate drift by progressively shortening or lengthening intervals while preserving all expected events. Demonstrate an omission by leaving one clap out while keeping subsequent claps on their original beats. Include correct examples so learners do not assume every demonstration is wrong.

Session 2: five minutes review, ten diagnose fresh examples, ten practise the corresponding repairs, and five reflect. For spacing errors, return to steady all-beat clapping with clicks before restoring the pattern. For omissions, speak all eight beat numbers and clap only paper-marked events, preserving silent positions. Alternate repairs and gradually remove the instructor’s verbal cue so learners choose from what they hear.

Session 3: five minutes review, ten use a listen–choose–retry cycle during group clapping, and fifteen complete the unfamiliar-pattern check. The instructor may identify the group error when it is audible, but should not attribute it to a learner. This approach primarily builds recognition and repair selection; accurate labels alone do not establish improved timing, and dense group sound may conceal omissions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before instruction and during session 3, present different short sets containing steady examples, drift, and omissions; tally anonymous choices to check listening discrimination. Then compare two unfamiliar, equally sparse eight-beat patterns. Give one a brief diagnosis-and-selected-repair cycle and the other equal-duration repetition with ‘try again’ feedback. Assess the next group attempt against the metronome, tallying omissions separately from drift. If identification improves but performance does not, the method has taught recognition without demonstrated correction. If selected repairs do no better than repetition, their added value remains unproven.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Fill the spaces, then fade the subdivision
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: insert quiet spoken halfway counts between beats, then gradually remove them. These intermediate time points may help beginners keep equal spacing across rests and avoid rushing toward the next clap. Paper separates expected claps from deliberate rests. The proposed benefit comes from subdividing long intervals into smaller, repeatable intervals.

Use only collective clapping, the instructor’s metronome, and paper strips showing eight numbered beats with clap marks. Everyone participates together; nobody demonstrates alone or receives named feedback. Assume learners can comfortably say ‘one-and, two-and’ at a slow tempo and hear the clicks beneath quiet speech. Subdivision can initially increase cognitive load, so introduce it on all-beat clapping before adding rests.

Session 1, 30 minutes: spend five minutes matching claps to clicks; five hearing instructor examples of tempo drift and missed claps; ten speaking numbers on clicks and ‘and’ halfway between them; and ten clapping marked beats while maintaining quiet subdivision. Explain that drift means successive claps move progressively ahead of or behind clicks. A missed clap leaves an expected position empty while later claps retain their timing. Deliberate paper-marked rests are neither error.

Session 2: five minutes review, fifteen alternate four repetitions with spoken subdivision and four with numbers alone, five practise recovery, and five reflect. For drift, restore even halfway counts. For a missed clap, continue counting and rejoin at the next marked position. Give only group feedback; call mixed or inaudible errors uncertain.

Session 3: ten minutes fade from spoken subdivision to silent counting, five rehearse familiar patterns without speech, and fifteen conduct the transfer check. This may support spacing, but dependence on speech or difficulty coordinating speech and claps could prevent transfer. Group sound also masks individual omissions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In session 3, introduce two unfamiliar eight-beat patterns matched for clap count and longest rest. Give each one metronome-supported baseline attempt. Draw lots to assign two minutes of subdivision practice to one and two minutes of ordinary numbered-count practice to the other. Then perform both without speech, with clicks audible. On paper, compare baseline-to-final changes in progressive displacement and clearly audible missing expected group claps separately; mark ambiguous cases uncertain. If subdivision yields no greater improvement, or adds omissions, its added value is unsupported in this rehearsal. Two patterns and collective observation provide only a preliminary check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep the motion through the rests
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: make clapping part of a continuous, comfortable hand movement. Hands approach on each beat and separate between beats; on a marked rest, make the same approach without contact. This gives silent positions a physical action, potentially preventing learners from shortening rests or losing their place. Gradually reduce the movement so the group can transfer the timing to ordinary clapping. The proposed mechanism is continuity of movement across silence.

Use the instructor’s metronome and paper showing eight numbered positions, with circles for claps and dashes for rests. Assume learners can comfortably make repeated small hand movements and hear the clicks. Allow a smaller movement where needed. All eight practise together; feedback concerns the group, with no solo demonstrations or named corrections.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes establish comfortable claps against clicks; five hear the instructor demonstrate tempo drift versus an omitted clap; ten establish the repeating approach-and-release motion; ten alternate claps and silent approaches using the paper. Explain that drift progressively moves attacks ahead of or behind clicks. A missed clap leaves an expected circle silent, while subsequent attacks may remain correctly timed. Printed rests are intentional.

Session 2: five minutes review; fifteen alternate ordinary clapping with continuous-motion rounds; five practise recovering after an omission without restarting; five reflect. For drift, restore a small, even movement against clicks. For omissions, follow the numbered positions and join the next circle. Keep movements relaxed rather than imposing a precise gesture shape.

Session 3: ten minutes progressively shrink the motion; five practise familiar patterns with ordinary clapping; fifteen check unfamiliar patterns. This could fail if coordinating silent approaches adds difficulty or if timing depends on conspicuous movement. Collective sound can conceal individual omissions, so conclusions concern audible group performance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Reserve two unfamiliar eight-beat patterns matched for clap count and rest length. During session 3, give each one ordinary-clapping baseline attempt with clicks. Draw lots: practise one for two minutes using continuous motion and the other for two minutes using ordinary clapping, with identical metronome support. Retest both using ordinary clapping. Tally clearly absent expected group attacks separately from progressive displacement against clicks; mark ambiguous cases uncertain. If motion practice produces no greater baseline-to-retest improvement, or increases omissions, its added value is unsupported here. This small comparison cannot establish individual improvement or rule out pattern differences.

EXPAND.title: Make the movement between claps carry the beat
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: use a continuous, repeatable hand movement to regulate the interval between claps. Beginners may rush because they prepare each clap separately; a small outward-and-return movement gives the time between sounds a consistent physical shape. This differs from maintaining pulse through silent metronome gaps: it changes how learners produce the intervals.

The instructor prepares paper strips showing eight numbered beats, with clap positions marked. Everyone works together at a comfortable metronome setting. On each beat, hands return to the same central position; they touch only at marked positions. At rests, hands complete the movement without contact. Keep movements small and comfortable; anyone uncomfortable can use a smaller version. No individual demonstrations or home practice are required.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes establish comfortable movement; five hear instructor examples of tempo drift and a missing clap; fifteen alternate ordinary clapping with continuous movement; five reflect on ease. Explain that progressively moving ahead of or behind the clicks indicates drift. A missing clap followed by correctly timed claps indicates an omitted event, not a faster tempo.

Session 2: five minutes review; fifteen practise patterns containing rests while preserving the movement; five reduce the movement size; five rehearse recovery. After an omission, keep the movement and rejoin at the next marked position. After drift, reset together against the clicks.

Session 3: five minutes warm up; ten gradually reduce visible movement; fifteen check unfamiliar patterns. The instructor gives only group feedback and marks uncertain observations as unclear.

Resources are clapping, paper, and the owned metronome. The main assumption is that movement can become regular without consuming excessive attention. It could instead increase fatigue or coordination demands. Improvement with large gestures may also fail to transfer to ordinary clapping.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor owns the trial. In session 3, introduce two unfamiliar patterns matched for length, rests, and clap count. By paper draw, assign one four-minute continuous-movement practice and the other four-minute silent-gap pulse practice from the prior route, with equal initial tempo support. Check both using ordinary group clapping against audible clicks, alternating order over two attempts. Tally progressive displacement and missing events separately; also collect private paper marks for comfort and effort. Retain the movement approach only provisionally if transfer is clearer without more omissions or discomfort. Stop the movement condition immediately for discomfort, or simplify after two rounds in which coordination breaks down. If ordinary-clapping performance is no better despite extra movement work, its added value is unsupported. Group masking and pattern differences limit this small comparison.

EXPAND.title: Reduce memory load by assembling the rhythm in chunks
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: make the event sequence easier to remember before combining it with steady timing. A beginner who is searching for the next clap position may hesitate and then rush to catch up. Learning short sections to continuity could prevent that source of unevenness. This changes sequence retrieval rather than dividing pulse duties or teaching error labels.

The instructor prepares eight-position paper patterns divided into two four-beat sections. Use only whole-beat claps and rests initially. Everyone sees the complete pattern throughout, so the method does not depend on reading notation or memorising a hidden score. The instructor explains that a printed rest is intentional, whereas a missing clap is silence at a marked position.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes establish pulse; five hear examples distinguishing progressive tempo drift from a missing event; ten practise the first and second sections separately with clicks; five join them; five reflect. Advance after two comfortable collective repetitions, without requiring perfection from every learner.

Session 2: five minutes review; ten assemble a new pattern; ten practise across the join, starting two beats before it and continuing two beats after it; five perform complete patterns. The bridge practice matters because isolated sections can otherwise create a pause at their boundary. For repeated omissions, return briefly to the relevant section. For progressive displacement, simplify to steady claps against clicks before rebuilding.

Session 3: five minutes warm up; ten assemble another pattern with progressively fewer pauses between sections; fifteen check unfamiliar material. All practice is collective, and feedback names positions or joins rather than people. If someone loses their place, they wait through the current section and rejoin at the next visible boundary while everyone else continues.

Resources are the instructor, metronome, clapping, and paper. The assumption is that sequence uncertainty contributes to the problem. This approach may offer little benefit when learners already know the sequence, and sectional practice can itself introduce boundary hesitations.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor runs a bounded comparison during session 3 using two unfamiliar eight-beat patterns matched for clap count and rests. Assign one by paper draw to four minutes of chunk-and-join practice; give the other four minutes of the prior listen–choose–repair approach. Perform both complete patterns twice against clicks, reversing order on the second pass. On paper, mark missing events, progressive displacement, and pauses at the section join separately. Ask learners privately whether the sequence felt easier to follow. Stop sectional repetition after two attempts that create an additional join pause and return to whole-pattern practice. The mechanism receives no practical support if omissions or timing do not improve, or if fewer omissions are offset by new boundary pauses. This small group check cannot establish individual mastery or eliminate pattern differences.

EXPAND.title: Show the group where time is with a continuous visual sweep
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: make current beat position visible while learners clap, reducing uncertainty about where the group is in the pattern. Unlike a static numbered strip, a moving reference lets learners notice that they have arrived early, late, or at the wrong position. Unlike a pulse subgroup, it provides the reference without adding another layer of clapping sound.

The instructor prepares a large paper row with eight equally spaced beat marks and marked clap positions. Everyone must be able to see it comfortably. With the metronome audible, the instructor moves a finger smoothly between successive marks, reaching each mark on its click. At the end, allow a separate reset count before beginning another eight-beat round; do not disguise the return sweep as performance time.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five minutes check visibility and establish pulse; five demonstrate drift versus an omitted clap; fifteen practise following the sweep through clap and rest positions; five discuss what was easy to follow. Drift means successive claps increasingly precede or follow the indicated beat. An omission leaves a marked event silent while later claps retain their positions.

Session 2: five minutes review; ten practise with the full sweep; ten alternate sweep-supported rounds with rounds using only the static paper and clicks; five practise recovery. If lost, keep listening and rejoin at the next round's start. For drift, reset against the metronome; for omissions, inspect the event marks before retrying. Feedback remains collective.

Session 3: five minutes warm up; ten progressively remove the sweep; fifteen test unfamiliar patterns without it. No learner is asked to perform alone.

The instructor must be able to point accurately while listening. If the sweep conflicts with clicks, stop and recalibrate; the visual cue must not become a competing tempo. The approach may reduce listening or create dependence on the instructor, so successful supported performance alone is insufficient.
EXPAND.experiment: The instructor compares the sweep with the prior shared-pulse-role approach during session 3. Use two unfamiliar patterns matched for length, clap count, and rests, assigning conditions by paper draw. Give each four minutes of practice, then have all eight learners perform each pattern together with static paper and audible metronome, without a sweep or pulse subgroup. Reverse test order for a second attempt. Tally progressive displacement and omitted events separately, and note lost-place restarts and whether learners found themselves watching instead of listening. Stop the sweep condition if the instructor cannot keep it aligned with clicks or if anyone cannot see comfortably. No added benefit is demonstrated if performance improves only while pointing continues, or if comparable transfer requires more instructor effort. This is a practical comparison, with uncertain results where group sound conceals errors.

EXPAND.title: Make listening evidence reliable before choosing a repair
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Hear the error, choose the repair.” Preserve its main mechanism: distinguish changing beat spacing from missing events, then apply the matching correction. Change the group-performance procedure because eight simultaneous clappers can conceal omissions and make repair selection unreliable.

The instructor assigns two groups of four by seating, rotating equally. One group claps while the other listens without producing a pulse; then they switch. Nobody performs alone or receives public individual feedback. Listeners privately mark paper with ‘spacing,’ ‘missing,’ ‘steady,’ or ‘unclear.’ This adds listening turns but reduces playing time; its value depends on clearer evidence leading to useful correction.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five establish pulse with the metronome; ten hear instructor examples of steady timing, progressive drift, and an omitted clap; ten alternate performing and listening; five review. Use visible eight-position patterns. A printed rest is intentional; an omission is silence at a marked clap position. Drift means successive events progressively move ahead of or behind clicks.

Session 2: five review; fifteen alternate listen–choose–repair–retry rounds; five combine all eight; five reflect. The instructor owns the repair decision. Apply a targeted repair only when the instructor hears the error and at least three listeners independently identify the same category. For drift, briefly clap every beat with clicks before restoring the pattern. For omissions, speak every position while clapping marked events. After one repair, retry the original pattern. If the error remains or evidence conflicts, stop repeating that repair: use a simpler complete pattern with audible clicks, then return once. Mixed errors receive this same fallback. Listener agreement supports a decision but does not prove accuracy.

Session 3: five review, ten repeat the cycle with fewer instructor prompts, fifteen check unfamiliar patterns. Resources are the owned metronome, clapping, and paper. Prerequisites are audible clicks and an instructor able to demonstrate clear examples. If examples cannot be distinguished, simplify them before advancing. Group sound still limits conclusions about individual mastery.
EXPAND.experiment:
The instructor runs the first bounded trial during session 2: allow four alternating performance/listening rounds within the allotted fifteen minutes. Note whether a supported diagnosis leads to a cleaner retry, recording omissions separately from progressive drift. If two rounds produce conflicting diagnoses or no usable decision, stop the listener-vote procedure and use instructor-led examples followed by simpler collective practice. This tests whether the extra listening time is worthwhile compared with ordinary whole-group repetition.

In session 3, introduce two previously unseen eight-position patterns matched for clap count and rests. Give each one baseline attempt, then equal practice time: use the revised listening procedure for one and whole-group repetition for the other, assigned by paper draw. Finish with all eight clapping each pattern against clicks. Tally omissions, progressive displacement, and unclear observations separately; collect private error-category marks after each attempt. Improvement requires both better listening choices and cleaner performance, not labels alone. Pattern differences, practice order, and masking prevent a strong causal conclusion.

EXPAND.title: Find a controllable tempo, then raise the demand gradually
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: adjust performance speed according to observed success. Uneven rhythm may reflect beginners having too little time to read, prepare, and coordinate each event. Instead of assuming the group must first acquire another timing aid, reduce the immediate demand, practise accurate whole patterns, and gradually restore speed. This differs from chunking because the complete sequence stays intact throughout.

The instructor uses the metronome and paper showing eight numbered positions with claps and rests. Everyone claps together; feedback concerns the group. Assume the metronome has adjustable tempo and at least one comfortable setting. Very slow tempos can also make pulse difficult, so slower is not automatically better.

Session 1, 30 minutes: five establish a comfortable pulse; five hear demonstrations distinguishing progressive drift from a missing event; fifteen find a workable tempo using short whole-pattern rounds; five review. Start at a pace the group can follow while counting aloud. After two rounds with no clearly audible group omission or progressive drift, increase by one small metronome step. After two rounds with the same clear error, return to the last successful setting. Unclear observations do not justify increasing speed.

Session 2: five review; twenty practise this tempo ladder on complete patterns; five reflect. The instructor controls changes and records only tempo, omissions, and drift. At each error, give the appropriate cue: ‘keep equal spacing’ for drift; ‘keep the beat positions and rejoin at the next marked clap’ for omissions. If returning to the last successful speed does not restore coordination within two attempts, simplify the complete pattern while retaining eight positions. If slowing makes timing worse, restore the previous pace instead of continuing downward. Never chase speed at the expense of stable performance.

Session 3: five warm up, ten practise with fewer tempo changes, fifteen check unfamiliar patterns at one fixed tempo. The intended gain is accurate timing that survives a new sequence. The shifted cost is fewer repetitions at the eventual rehearsal pace and possible dependence on easier tempos. No home equipment, individual demonstration, or public learner ranking is needed.
EXPAND.experiment:
The instructor first tries the ladder for ten minutes within session 1. Stop increasing speed after the first repeated breakdown; allow at most two downward adjustments before using the simpler-pattern fallback. If no setting permits coordinated rounds, suspend the ladder and spend the remaining practice time establishing a steady pulse with audible clicks. Record this as failure to establish its prerequisite, not learner failure.

For the session 3 check, choose a fixed tempo demonstrated as workable during session 2. Introduce two unfamiliar eight-position patterns matched for claps and rests and take one baseline attempt of each at that tempo. Assign one by paper draw to three minutes of tempo-ladder practice and the other to three minutes of practice at the fixed tempo. Test both again at the fixed tempo, with all eight clapping and clicks audible. Record omissions and progressive drift separately, alongside time spent below the check tempo. The ladder has provisional practical value only if timing improves on unfamiliar material without increasing omissions; success solely at a slower test speed would not establish transfer. This small comparison cannot establish individual improvement or eliminate pattern differences.
